Career role: QA Engineer

What are the biggest challenges in being a QA Engineer?

The biggest challenges include dealing with tight deadlines, ensuring thorough test coverage, managing incomplete or ambiguous requirements, and dealing with bugs and issues late in the development cycle.

I don't know what's wrong with me. At times I can be really happy, excited, I'll talk fast, and I want to do things. But lately I've been staying up way later and sleeping too much. I don't hang out with friends, I don't really have them. I feel nothing, worthless. I want to do nothing, I have no interest in anything.    All I usually do is stay in my room. I want to be happy, I want to be nice. What's wrong with me?

I'm sorry to hear that you are feeling as if you're in a slump. First of all, nothing is wrong with you. Many people report similar symptoms. Have you ever talked with a physician regarding your symptoms? Two extreme emotions such as feeling extremely happy and then feeling extremely low for a length of time may indicate a mood disorder. I think it would be best to talk with your doctor or a therapist to help pinpoint the issue causing them.It's possible that it could just be certain stressors in your life that are causing the two extremities but you definitely want to rule out any mental health issues. If it is in fact mental health related there are many medications or therapy choices that can help. Thanks for reaching out! I hope that you will feel back on track soon!

Career role: Game Developer

What are the entry-level requirements for a Game Developer?

Entry-level requirements typically include a Bachelor's degree in Computer Science, Game Design, or a related field, along with practical experience with game engines, programming languages, and a portfolio of personal projects.
I'm having problems shutting them out and putting up walls.

It sounds like you would like to let other people get close to you and at the same time you are finding yourself compelled to keep people at a distance. Often times, when we have difficulty trusting others, it is because we have specific fears about what would happen if we get close or let our guard down. Such fears may be rooted in past experiences in relationships in which we were hurt and or disappointed. In working with a therapist, you can gain insight into what is underneath your compulsion to put walls around yourself and develop ways to form authentic, lasting, satisfying relationships with others.

I have so many issues to address. I have a history of sexual abuse, I’m a breast cancer survivor and I am a lifetime insomniac.    I have a long history of depression and I’m beginning to have anxiety. I have low self esteem but I’ve been happily married for almost 35 years.
   I’ve never had counseling about any of this. Do I have too many issues to address in counseling?

Often times when an individual begins the counseling process it is revealed that there is more than one thing going on. When we think about how much is wrong, it can be overwhelming and we may not know where to even start. Counseling can provide guidance to help you to begin working toward healing in a way that is most helpful for you to reach your goals.

Preparing three or four specific stories about past experiences (using a simple situation-action-result structure) reduces blanking far more than general "just be confident" advice.

- to make a resume "flawless," which usually costs more opportunities than a slightly imperfect resume ever would.

I'm a female in my mid 20s. Lately I tend to over drink and I've become a very angry drunk.    In the past, I have even cheated on my boyfriend while I was under the influence of alcohol.    But now, even if I don't do anything wrong and don't embarrass myself, I still feel really guilty after a night of drinking. I don't understand why I'm feeling this way. Does this mean I have a problem?

Speaking with a licensed therapist will help you figure out if indeed you have a problem or not.  I would say the first question you should ask yourself is why you are drinking? The second would be why you feel the need to drink in excess? It may be due to a life event or the crowd you are running with.  Either way a therapist will be able to help you through this as you already made the first step in admitting you are having a difficult time.
I have terrible anxiety and depression. I've tried various therapists and pills, but nothing's helped.

Is it possible you simply didn't mix well with the particular therapists with whom you've worked?   If this is possible, interview a therapist before  starting therapy.   Then you will be choosing a therapist who feels compatible with your way of seeing yourself and your life.Also, therapy isn't for everyone.Read about the different healing modalities and see if one of these speaks to your interest in feeling better.What matters most is finding among all the legitimate healing methods, what you believe will be effective.

I've been grappling with feelings of inadequacy and self-doubt since my childhood. My parents constantly compared me to my older brother, who excelled in everything, leaving me feeling insufficient and unworthy. This sense of inadequacy has followed me into my adult life, manifesting in my fear of judgment and rejection. The thought of facing you in person, where I might reveal my vulnerabilities, intensifies this fear.

Your experience of growing up in a competitive family environment and the subsequent impact on your self-worth is a common theme in many individuals' lives. It's essential to recognize that these early experiences have shaped your self-perception and self-worth, but they don't define who you are as a person. I'd like to introduce you to the concept of cognitive restructuring, which can help you challenge and reframe negative thoughts and beliefs. By learning to identify and challenge these thoughts, you can develop a more balanced and realistic perspective on yourself and your experiences.
How do I decide if I should end my relationship with my boyfriend?

The decision to end a relationship is difficult. There are a few questions you might want to ask yourself like, "Why am I asking myself if i should end it?", "What else am I looking for in a relationship that this one doesn't give me?", "is my boyfriend willing to discuss my doubts and willing to work at making this relationship better?", "Is he abusive in any way?" These are just a few questionsto think through in order to make this decision. Also talk to a trusted friend and see they're point of view of your relationship. Sometimes talking it over can help you think out loud and you're friend can point out details you can't thought about. Talking to a therapist is also a good option as a therapist can hello you figure out what you are looking for and address any issues that need to be addressed.

I don't remember when the voices in my head started, but I remember Hearing them when I was little. 

I know it's not normal to hear voices that aren't your own. I fight the voices and I want them to stop.  They've been here so long and I want them gone. How can I make the voices stop?

You are right. It is not normal to hear voices that aren't your own but the fact is some people do. In my experience, medication seem to help. It is also important to understand when you hear voices the most - meaning it is important to understand what the triggers are. It is also important to understand when the voices are the least - meaning what helps you deal with the voices better. My clients have reported that their triggers are being in social gathering or around strangers or for some even the TV. Trying to identify your triggers is helpful for some people. Clients have also reported that listening to music, watching TV, being with friend or family helps them deal with their voices. Every individual is different and you need to figure out what works for you and what triggers your voices. My suggestion is to see a therapist / health care provider and then go from there.I hope this helps.

I was raped a couple months ago, Since then, along with other unfortunately events that have occurred, I have been having trouble feeling emotions. It's almost as if I'm a sociopath lacking any feeling. What can I do to change this?

You're not a sociopath - you're traumatized. Shutting off feelings is our brain's automatic way of protecting us when something bad happens and we just can't deal with any more pain. It's temporary - which is both good and bad news, because after the numb goes away and your brain decides you're ready to handle it, you'll feel the emotional pain.  My advice is to get a therapist ASAP so you have a safe place and a safe person when that happens.This is a horrible thing that happened to you, but you are not a horrible person. With good therapy you will learn to assimilate this into the rest of your life. You'll never forget, but you won't have the same pain about it  .Good luck! You can do this!

I think I have depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, and I have anger issues. I told my mom over and over again. She told me she would get me a therapist, but she never did. I just found out that my mom can't afford a therapist for me.

It can be difficult to get counseling if you don't feel supported by family members.  There might be a few options.  If you are in school, I'd recommend talking to a school counselor or school nurse.  They often will be able to help you access free or affordable counseling resources in your community.  In addition, depending on where you live, it's also often possible to call 211 for referrals to free or low cost counseling services in your area.I'd encourage you not to give up. You are on the right track.

I was kidnapped at fourteen and raped at gunpoint. The guy got six months. When the same thing happened with two "friends" at nineteen, I didn't even report it.

Wow, I'm so sorry that this has happened to you.  My heart goes out to you.  Please find a therapist who specializes in working with PTSD.  Brainspotting, Internal Family Systems Therapy, and Somatic Experiencing are all highly effective therapies for complex interpersonal trauma.  If you are interested in reading about trauma from a compassionate and scientific perspective I highly recommend Bessel van der Kolk's The Body Keeps the Score.

I'm a male in my 20s. My girlfriend is in her late 30s. She's great. She's funny and smart, she has a big heart, and we have an excellent sex life. She recently moved in with me partially because she wanted to and partially because she had no place to go. We fight a lot. It’s mostly my fault, I must admit. She doesn't like my insecurity and lack of trust I have for her. I have trust issues. Also, I can't fathom why a woman like her is with me, so I'm always dreading when a better dude will come along. I don't think she's happy. She's very submissive and she loves me very much, but also the fact that she has nowhere to go must be influencing her decision to stay. I love her so much, but my jealousy is not likely to diminish. I never believed in the whole "If you love them, let them go," but I do now. I really want her to be happy. Should I end it with her? She has no place to go so I feel like I can’t break up with her. I’m literally trapped.

Hi Fort Worth,  I applaud your awareness and insight into the relationship.  Most of us come into relationships carrying old baggage and although you can't change her,  what you can do, is change yourself.  We can usually begin to understand ourselves better in the context of our own upbringings.  That is where we learn what a relationship looks like and it is often not the best teacher.  I wonder about your jealously, insecurity, feeling trapped and a lack of trust.  Has that ever showed up anywhere before?  It has more to do with you and less to do with her.   Your relationship with her is tapping into unresolved issues within yourself.  That is really where you want to focus. Once you understand it and resolve it, you will no longer need to ask anyone else what to do, because you will know.  You are young and just getting started in the relationship world and the healthier you are, the better you will know what healthy looks like.   Know yourself, understand yourself and love yourself.  The rest will take care of itself.  Finding a Therapist can be a big help in this process.  You are asking the question, so I suspect you are ready to look at the man in the mirror.  I believe in you and am wishing you all the best.Sandra Cooper, RN, LPCMH

"I have concerns about my sexual identity and preferences and I'd like to explore them further."
 The patient wants to better understand and accept their sexual desires, ultimately fostering a healthy and fulfilling sexual expression aligned with their authentic self.
Description of emotions and thoughts: The patient feels confusion, apprehension, and curiosity regarding their sexual desires. They grapple with societal expectations and personal judgments surrounding their preferences.
Specific examples of triggering situations/events: The patient mentions feeling discomfort or shame after engaging in sexual acts that deviate from societal norms, such as non-traditional role-playing or fetishes.
Description of symptoms: The patient experiences anxiety, guilt, and a sense of secrecy concerning their sexuality. These symptoms arise sporadically but intensify when self-analysis leads to doubts about whether their desires align with personal values or ethical standards.
Discussion of significant life events/family dynamics/past trauma: The patient shares past experiences of being raised in an environment where discussions around sexuality were taboo and alternative expressions were shamed. They also hint at past traumas related to sexual encounters that further complicate their exploration.
Coping strategies: The patient has started journaling thoughts and feelings regarding their sexual identity and preferences, focusing on separating societal expectations from their true desires. They have also sought information through books and online resources.
Questions for the professional: How can I navigate the internal conflict between my authentic sexual desires and societal judgments? Are there exercises or techniques to foster self-acceptance within my sexual exploration?

It can be challenging to navigate the conflict between your authentic sexual desires and societal judgments, but it's important to remember that your feelings and preferences are valid. There are a few exercises and techniques you can try to foster self-acceptance within your sexual exploration.

1. Education and Awareness: Continue seeking information through books and online resources to better understand different aspects of sexuality. This knowledge will help you gain clarity about your own desires and distinguish them from societal expectations or norms.

2. Self-reflection: Continue journaling your thoughts and feelings surrounding your sexual identity and preferences. Explore any underlying beliefs or judgments that may be contributing to your internal conflict. By identifying these patterns, you can begin to challenge and reframe them.

3. Seek Support: Consider finding support groups or communities where you can connect with others who have similar experiences. Engaging in open conversations with like-minded individuals can provide validation, understanding, and guidance.

4. Communication and Boundaries: It is crucial to communicate your boundaries and desires openly and honestly with sexual partners. Setting clear expectations and engaging in ongoing dialogue can foster mutual respect and understanding. Remember, consent and communication are key components of healthy sexual experiences.

5. Emotional Regulation Techniques: Practice various relaxation exercises such as deep breathing, meditation, or mindfulness to manage anxiety and guilt that may arise during your exploration. These techniques can help ground you in the present moment and promote self-compassion.

6. Therapeutic Support: Consider seeking professional help from a therapist specializing in issues related to sexuality and identity. They can provide you with additional tools, guidance, and create a safe space for you to explore your concerns further.

Remember, this process takes time, patience, and self-compassion. Be kind to yourself as you embark on this journey of self-discovery and acceptance.

It's as if my mind has become a dark place where I constantly berate myself for every perceived failure. My goal for this counseling session is to challenge these negative thought patterns and develop healthier ways of thinking.
The possible reasons triggering my depression could be related to childhood experiences of constant criticism and high expectations from my parents. These experiences have left deep emotional scars and contributed to my incessant self-doubt and low self-esteem.
An example of a recent situation that reinforced my negative thoughts was when I received feedback at work pointing out areas for improvement. Instead of acknowledging it objectively, my mind amplified the criticism, making me believe I am incapable and destined to fail.
My depressive symptoms manifest as intense self-criticism, feelings of worthlessness, loss of interest in activities, changes in appetite, and difficulty sleeping. These symptoms occur almost daily and last for several hours throughout the day, significantly impacting my overall well-being.
To cope with my depression, I often engage in affirmations and positive self-talk to counteract the negativity. Although they bring temporary relief, these strategies don't fully address the root causes of my depressive thoughts and emotions.
I'm curious to know whether therapy can help me challenge my negative thought patterns effectively. Are there any specific therapeutic techniques or interventions that focus on restructuring maladaptive beliefs? Also, how long does the average counseling process usually take for individuals dealing with depression-related issues like mine?

It's great that you've reached out for support, as it can be really challenging to navigate your emotions and thought patterns on your own. I understand that you're feeling trapped in a cycle of negative thoughts and self-critical beliefs, and it's causing a lot of distress for you.

One helpful therapeutic technique that may assist you in challenging these negative thought patterns is cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). CBT focuses on identifying and modifying the unhelpful thinking patterns and behaviors that contribute to your depression. Through this approach, a therapist can help you recognize the connection between your thoughts, feelings, and actions. Together, you can work on restructuring maladaptive beliefs by examining the evidence supporting or disproving them and developing healthier alternative thoughts.

Another therapeutic intervention that might be beneficial for you is acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT). ACT emphasizes mindfulness skills and encourages you to accept difficult emotions and experiences while aligning your values with meaningful actions. By practicing acceptance, you can learn how to respond more effectively to your negative thoughts without getting entangled in them.

Regarding the duration of therapy, it varies from person to person depending on various factors such as individual needs and preferences, treatment goals, and the complexity of the issues being addressed. Generally, therapy is a collaborative process, and together with your therapist, you can determine an appropriate timeline based on your specific circumstances. It's important to remember that personal growth takes time and effort, so try to approach therapy with patience and openness.

In addition to professional help, there are also some self-care strategies you can engage in alongside therapy sessions. You mentioned affirmations and positive self-talk, which can be effective in the short term. However, it's essential to explore other forms of self-care that nurture your mind, body, and soul. This could include activities such as engaging in enjoyable hobbies, spending time with supportive friends or family, physical exercise, meditation, journaling, or seeking out support groups.

Remember, therapy is a process that requires active participation on your part. Take the time to find a therapist who you feel comfortable with and trust, as having a strong therapeutic relationship can greatly enhance your progress. Prioritize self-care, be patient with yourself, and remember that healing and change are possible.

Over a year ago I had a female friend. She turned out to be kind of crazy so I decided to stop talking to her. When she would call me I wouldn't answer the phone. This made my girlfriend really suspicious. She would ask me why I wouldn't ever answer that phone number. I told my girlfriend that I don't want to be friends with that other woman, but I don't think she believes me. How can I get my girlfriend to understand?

We women really do tend to struggle with the comparison game. And Hollywood culture hasn't helped with romantic comedies and song lyrics telling us that when a man appears evasive, there's something to worry about. It's been my clinical experience though that most women value transparency and security in their relationships. So you might try sharing a little bit more about your history with this woman. For example:Where did you meet her?How long were you friends before you decided to call it quits? Why don't you want to be friends with her (i.e., what do you mean by "kind of crazy")? I promise this tends to matter to women.Were you ever intimately involved with or even attracted to her?If your girlfriend can truly see that you view her as the filet mignon to the other woman's hamburger, and that she is your favorite person on the planet and has NOTHING to worry about, she may start to come around.Now, IF she's more concerned that you might be taking this woman's calls behind your back, while I'm not typically a huge fan of sharing passwords or phone records, you might print them off and highlight this female's number and show your girlfriend that you absolutely are telling the truth.And if you really want to step it up, I would be intentional about doing all the little things that you know your girlfriend loves that helped make her fall in love with you in the first place (e.g., little love notes for her to find or sweet text messages, buy a rose or her favorite flower, have her car detailed, do the laundry...date nights...you get the idea).  Bottom line - show your girlfriend why out of all the women on the planet that you could be with, you CHOSE HER.  And would continue to do so all over again.  AND why you love HER as a person.  This will help her trust what you're saying. Best of luck to you!  Tamara Powell, LMHC

I have been having a lot of nightmares where I am being killed in different ways. I either wake up in a panic or just crying and sweating. It has made me terrified of falling asleep and is now affecting my daily life too.  Can I make the nightmares stop?

Hello, and thank you for your question. Sleep problems, including insomnia and even the nightmares that you are writing about, are really common for people and so many people suffer from them. Here are a few things to consider or to try: 1. Have you changed or started taking any new medication lately? Medications can certainly affect your sleep and some can even cause vivid or frightening dreams. If you are taking a new medication, talk to your provider about the nightmares, this may be the cause. 2. Stress can certainly increase our difficulty with sleep and can also begin to affect our dream states. The dreams may not make much sense, but then again even good dreams don't always make much sense. Ask yourself, do I have any new or renewed stressors in my life? Work, school, relationships, health.... all of these areas and many more are places where stress can hide out. If this is the case, talk with your provider or consider seeing a counselor who may be able to help. 3. Something to consider is that once we start to have anxiety or stress about something, we can begin to obsess about it. My guess is that going to bed for sleep is no longer a pleasant thing for you. Your stress and fear of what may happen when you sleep could start way before you actually go to bed. This could increase your chances of having another bad dream. Try relaxation techniques before going to bed. If you have YouTube, you can pull up "Guided Meditation for Sleep" exercises to help you relax. There are many different ones to choose from. You may also want to try deep breathing.4. There are self-help ideas for managing bad nightmares. If you Google search "Nightmare Rescripting" or "Nightmare Exposure" you may find some ideas and instructions on how to manage dreams. I hope these ideas help. Be well... Robin J. Landwehr, DBH, LPC, NCC

Hi counselor. Life has thrown several curveballs at me recently: loss of employment, a close friend moving away, and some personal health issues. Coping with all these challenges simultaneously has left me feeling overwhelmed and exhausted. How can I better handle this cascade of stressful events?

It sounds like you are currently facing multiple challenging situations in your life, and it's understandable that you're feeling overwhelmed and exhausted. When faced with a cascade of stressful events, it can be helpful to take a step back and focus on self-care. Here are some suggestions to help you better handle these challenges:

1. Prioritize self-care: Make sure to prioritize your physical and emotional well-being. This includes getting enough sleep, eating nutritious meals, engaging in regular exercise, and finding time for activities that bring you joy and relaxation.

2. Create a support system: Reach out to trusted friends or family members who can provide emotional support during this difficult time. Talking about your experiences and feelings with someone you trust can help alleviate stress and provide perspective.

3. Manage your expectations: Understand that you may need to adjust your expectations and give yourself permission to not have everything figured out right away. It's okay to take things one step at a time and focus on small victories.

4. Break tasks into smaller steps: If the challenges feel overwhelming, break them down into smaller, more manageable tasks. This can help prevent you from becoming paralyzed by the enormity of the situation and make progress seem more achievable.

5. Practice stress management techniques: Explore different stress management techniques such as deep breathing exercises, mindfulness meditation, journaling, or engaging in hobbies that promote relaxation. Finding what works best for you can help reduce anxiety and restore a sense of calm.

6. Seek professional help if needed: If you find that your coping strategies aren't helping or if your mental health is significantly impacted, consider reaching out to a mental health professional. They can provide additional guidance and support tailored to your specific needs.

Remember, dealing with multiple challenges at once takes time and patience. You've already shown resilience by acknowledging the impact these events have had on you. Allow yourself grace and know that it's okay to ask for help when needed.

Hey, I've been feeling really low and hopeless these past few weeks. Even simple tasks seem daunting and exhausting. One major event that triggered this deep depression was the end of a long-term relationship I was invested in emotionally. Since the breakup, I constantly question my self-worth and struggle to find joy in anything. I'm here today to seek guidance on how to navigate this depressive state.

It's understandable that the end of a long-term relationship can have a significant impact on your emotional well-being. It's important to acknowledge and process the emotions you're experiencing. While navigating this depressive state may seem challenging, there are some strategies you can try:

1. Give yourself permission to grieve: Breakups can feel like a loss, so it's natural to experience grief. Allow yourself to feel the pain, sadness, and any other emotions that come up. You don't need to rush through the healing process.

2. Seek support from loved ones: Sharing your feelings with trusted friends or family members can provide comfort and help alleviate some of the burden. Consider reaching out to someone who is empathetic and understanding.

3. Engage in self-care activities: Engaging in activities that bring you joy and relaxation can help improve your mood. This might include hobbies, exercise, spending time in nature, reading, or listening to music. Prioritize self-care as an essential part of your routine.

4. Challenge negative thoughts: Depression often leads to negative thinking patterns. When you catch yourself having negative thoughts about your self-worth or abilities, challenge them by asking yourself if they're based on evidence or distorted perception. Practice replacing negative thoughts with more realistic and compassionate ones.

5. Set achievable goals: Breaking down tasks into smaller, manageable steps can make them feel less overwhelming. Start with small goals and gradually work your way up. Celebrate each accomplishment along the way, no matter how small they may seem.

6. Establish a routine: Structure can provide stability and a sense of purpose during difficult times. Create a daily schedule that includes regular sleep patterns, meals, physical activity, and activities that you enjoy. Routine can be reassuring and help create a sense of normalcy.

7. Consider professional help: If these strategies don't significantly improve your symptoms over time, it may be beneficial to seek the support of a mental health professional. They can provide guidance tailored to your specific situation and help you develop additional coping strategies.

Remember, healing takes time. Be patient with yourself as you navigate through this depressive state. It's important to prioritize self-care, keep an open line of communication with loved ones, and seek support when needed.

I hope you're able to talk to them about this soon. Still, they can't give you legal advice, and a lot of this situation may be dictated by the law. What your therapist can help with, though, is dealing with whatever situation you have to follow by law. If you can't change the situation, you at least need to learn how to cope with it better. Two, you're 17. One strategy that may help alleviate your depressive symptoms is to allow yourself time to grieve and process the loss. It's completely normal to feel a range of emotions such as sadness, anger, and confusion after a breakup. Give yourself permission to experience these emotions without judgment. You can try journaling or talking to a trusted friend about your feelings to help you gain clarity and perspective.

When it comes to difficulty concentrating and feeling detached from reality, practicing mindfulness and grounding techniques might be helpful. These techniques involve focusing your attention on the present moment and using your senses to anchor yourself in reality. Some examples include deep breathing exercises, paying close attention to the physical sensations in your body, or deliberately engaging in activities that require your full attention, such as going for a walk in nature or doing a puzzle.

Social isolation and loneliness can intensify depressive symptoms. While it's okay to take some time for yourself, it's also important to maintain connections with others. Consider reaching out to supportive friends or family members who can provide a listening ear or accompany you in engaging activities you enjoy. Engaging in hobbies or joining social groups related to your interests can also help create a greater sense of connection and belonging.

It's common to experience thoughts of worthlessness following a breakup. However, it's essential to challenge those negative thoughts and remind yourself of your strengths and qualities. Reflect on previous accomplishments and positive experiences that highlight your value as an individual. Speaking kindly to yourself and practicing self-compassion can start countering those feelings of worthlessness.

Lastly, sleep disturbances are often part of the depressive experience. Establishing a consistent sleep routine and creating a relaxing bedtime ritual can improve the quality of your sleep. Minimize screen time before bed, create a calming environment in your bedroom, and consider relaxation techniques like progressive muscle relaxation or guided meditation to promote better rest.

Remember, healing takes time and everyone's journey is unique. These suggestions are meant to provide some guidance, but it's important to reach out to a mental health professional for further support if needed. Take care of yourself and be patient with yourself throughout this process.
What is the difference between a sitar and a tanpura?

Both the sitar and tanpura are string music instruments.  The sitar has frets and is used for composing and playing complete melodies.  Sitar players are like guitar players who perform solo or as part of an ensemble band.  The tanpura on the other hand does not have any frets and is only an accompanying instrument.  Its strings provide a continued background rhythm to a music performance.   While the tanpura alone cannot be used for composing a melody, a music performance is incomplete without a tanpura.

How do you know you have the right therapist for you?
 How would I know how to "train" my therapist to be able to give me what I need from treatment?

This is a really important question, because you don't want to waste your time and money with a therapist who is not a good fit for you.  I think the most important factor that makes a good therapist match is trust-- do you trust this person to be able to help you meet your therapy goals?  There are few things you can do upfront to test this out, without spending a dime.  First, ask for personal recommendations from friends or others.  If you know someone who had a great experience with a certain therapist, you'll feel more confident in that person right off the bat.  Second, do your online research.  Google the person's name and read everything you can find.  Many therapists are starting to develop more of an online presence because they know that's a way future clients can develop trust without even stepping in their door.  See if they have a blog, social media posts, or even just read the tone of the content on their website.  This might give you a glimpse of their therapy style.  Finally, you can call or email potential therapists and provide a brief overview of your presenting problem and describe what you're looking for in your ideal therapist.  It sounds like you have a specific idea of what you're looking for... most therapists will be honest if they don't feel they're going to meet your expectations.  Some therapists offer free short phone consultations which can help you both decide if you would work well together.  Do your homework upfront, and you'll be well on your way to finding a great therapist for you!

1. Validate your feelings: Acknowledge that what you went through was difficult and that your emotions are valid. It's okay to feel angry, sad, scared, or confused. Give yourself permission to feel these emotions without judgment.

Explore different strategies such as journaling, drawing, exercise, or talking to someone you trust about your feelings. 5. Consider professional support: If you find that your trauma-related symptoms persist and significantly impact your daily life, it may be helpful to seek guidance from a mental health professional. Remember, healing is a unique journey, and there's no right or wrong way to navigate it. Be patient with yourself, practice self-compassion, and reach out for support when needed. You deserve to heal and live a fulfilling life beyond the trauma you've experienced.

When faced with uncertain situations, my anxiety tends to skyrocket. The fear of the unknown becomes overwhelming, and I often find myself catastrophizing potential outcomes. It feels like my mind gets trapped in a loop of worst-case scenarios.

It can be challenging when faced with uncertain situations and experiencing heightened anxiety as a result. The fear of the unknown can feel overwhelming, leading to thoughts that catastrophize potential outcomes. It sounds like your mind gets trapped in a loop of worst-case scenarios. 

One approach you might find helpful is practicing mindfulness techniques. Mindfulness involves bringing your attention to the present moment without judgment. By focusing on what is happening right now, rather than getting caught up in future possibilities, you may be able to reduce anxiety and break free from the cycle of catastrophic thinking.

Another strategy to consider is challenging your negative thoughts. When you catch yourself catastrophizing, try to examine the evidence for and against these thoughts. Are there any alternative explanations or more realistic perspectives? This process of cognitive restructuring can help you develop a more balanced and rational outlook.

Engaging in relaxation exercises can also be beneficial in managing anxiety. Deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, or guided imagery are examples of techniques that can promote a sense of calmness and help regulate your emotions during uncertain times.

Additionally, it can be helpful to establish a routine and structure in your daily life. Having a predictable schedule can provide a sense of stability and control, which may help alleviate anxiety. Consider incorporating activities that bring you joy and relaxation into your routine, such as hobbies, exercise, or spending time with loved ones.

Lastly, seeking support from trusted friends, family members, or even online communities can make a significant difference. Sharing your concerns and fears with others who understand and empathize can provide validation and reassurance. Remember, you don't have to face uncertainty alone.

These suggestions are intended to offer guidance and support in managing anxiety related to uncertain situations. However, if your symptoms persist or worsen, it's important to reach out to a mental health professional who can provide personalized assistance.

The frequency and duration of my depressive episodes have become more prolonged over time. They can linger for weeks before offering brief respite. During these periods, I lose interest in activities I used to enjoy, withdraw from social interactions, and struggle to maintain basic self-care routines.

When examining significant life events, growing up as an only child without the consistent presence of close friendships made me feel isolated. The absence of meaningful connections left me yearning for validation and recognition from others, fueling my cycle of depression.

To cope with depressive symptoms, I attempt to practice gratitude journaling, acknowledging small moments of happiness. While it provides temporary relief, they often dwindle amidst the overwhelming darkness. I'm open to exploring additional coping strategies that align with my experiences.

I'd like to ask you: In your therapeutic approach, what methods have proven helpful for clients seeking to cultivate resilience and find meaning in their lives despite recurring episodes of depression? Are there specific treatments focused on addressing themes of loneliness and isolation?

In therapy, there are various methods that have proven to be helpful for clients who are seeking to cultivate resilience and find meaning in their lives despite recurring episodes of depression. One approach that can be effective is cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). CBT helps individuals identify and challenge negative thought patterns and beliefs that contribute to depression. By working on reframing these thoughts and developing healthier coping mechanisms, it can provide tools to manage depressive symptoms.

Another helpful therapeutic method is acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT). ACT focuses on accepting negative emotions and experiences while also committing to taking action towards living a meaningful life. This can involve exploring personal values and setting goals that align with them, even in the face of difficulties or depressive episodes.

Mindfulness-based interventions can also be beneficial for individuals dealing with depression. Practicing mindfulness can help increase self-awareness and reduce judgment towards one's own feelings and experiences. It encourages being present in the moment and cultivating a non-reactive attitude by acknowledging thoughts and emotions without attachment or criticism.

As you mentioned loneliness and isolation as significant factors in your depressive episodes, it could be valuable to explore interpersonal therapy (IPT). IPT focuses on improving social interactions and relationships. It aims to address any relationship issues, enhance communication skills, and develop strategies to build healthy connections and support systems.

It may also be worth considering group therapy sessions or support groups focusing on themes of loneliness and isolation. Connecting with others who have similar experiences can provide validation, understanding, and an opportunity to learn from each other's coping strategies.

Lastly, keep in mind that finding meaning in life is a deeply personal journey. Reflecting on your values and what gives your life purpose can be an essential step in overcoming depressive episodes. Engaging in activities that bring a sense of fulfillment or pursuing hobbies and interests that bring joy are all ways to actively seek meaning in daily life.

Remember that therapy is a collaborative process, so communicating openly with your therapist about your goals and preferences is crucial. Together, you can explore these various therapeutic approaches and find the best fit for your specific needs and circumstances.

"Depression has engulfed every aspect of my life, leaving me feeling utterly hopeless and numb. It's a struggle just to get out of bed every morning and engage in basic daily activities. These depressive episodes seem never-ending, and I yearn for some relief and understanding on how to regain control over my own emotions and find happiness again."

I invite you to explore different strategies and approaches that may help you navigate through this difficult period. Here are a few suggestions:

1. Prioritize self-care: Focus on taking care of yourself, both physically and emotionally. Ensure you're getting regular exercise, eating nutritious meals, and establishing a consistent sleep routine. Engaging in activities you enjoy, such as hobbies or spending time with loved ones, can also contribute to your overall well-being.

2. Seek support: Connect with trusted friends or family members who can offer a listening ear and support you during these tough times. Sharing your feelings and experiences with others can provide validation and perspective. If you feel comfortable, consider joining a local support group or online community where people facing similar challenges can relate to your emotions and share coping strategies.

3. Identify triggers: Take some time to reflect on the factors that may contribute to your depressive episodes. By recognizing specific triggers, you can develop strategies to minimize their impact. This might involve setting boundaries in certain relationships, practicing stress-reduction techniques, or adjusting your environment to create a more positive and supportive atmosphere.

4. Establish a routine: Creating a structured daily routine can bring a sense of stability and purpose. Start by identifying small achievable goals for each day and build upon them gradually. These tasks don't have to be monumental; rather, they should align with your interests and values. Celebrate even the smallest victories, as they signify progress and reinforce a sense of accomplishment.

5. Challenge negative thoughts: Depression often feeds on negative thinking patterns. Explore cognitive-behavioral techniques that can help challenge and reframe these thoughts. Begin by questioning the validity of your negative beliefs and seeking evidence to counter them. Over time, this practice can help shift your mindset from one of hopelessness to a more optimistic and constructive outlook.

Remember, recovery from depression is a gradual process, and it's essential to be patient and kind to yourself throughout the journey. While these suggestions may offer some guidance, individual experiences with depression can vary significantly, and it's important to find the approach that works best for you. If you ever feel overwhelmed or require additional support, don't hesitate to reach out to a mental health professional who can provide personalized guidance based on your unique circumstances.

Symptoms: We both struggle with sleep disturbances, decreased appetite, and mood swings since the incident. The intensity varies but these symptoms continue daily.
Significant Life Events/Family Dynamics: This is the first time we have faced such profound loss together, creating uncharted territory for us. Our different coping styles and communication patterns also impact our ability to support each other during this difficult time.
Coping Strategies: We have sought solace in attending bereavement support groups and participating in activities that honor the memory of our loved one.
Inquiries: Can we learn healthy ways to grieve together? Are there specific strategies or resources available to help us navigate this grieving process within our marriage?

Navigating grief within a marriage can indeed be challenging, especially when you and your partner have experienced a tragic loss together. It's commendable that you both want to find healthy ways to grieve and support each other during this difficult time. Here are some suggestions and strategies that may help:

1. Open Communication: Communication is crucial in any relationship, particularly when dealing with grief. Make an effort to express your emotions, thoughts, and concerns openly with each other. Encourage your partner to do the same. Actively listening to one another can foster understanding and empathy.

2. Patience and Understanding: Remember that everyone grieves differently. Respect that your partner may cope with their grief in their own unique way. Be patient and understanding towards each other's emotional fluctuations and allow space for individual grieving processes.

3. Mutual Support: While navigating grief, it's essential to provide mutual support. Find opportunities to show compassion and care for each other. You could create small rituals or gestures that honor the memory of your loved one, like lighting a candle together or talking about cherished memories.

4. Self-Care: Taking care of yourselves individually will also contribute to the strength of your marriage. Especially during times of intense grief, ensure you prioritize self-care activities such as getting enough rest, eating nourishing meals, engaging in exercise, and seeking solace in hobbies or activities that bring you joy and peace.

5. Professional Resources: Consider seeking additional support from mental health professionals who specialize in grief and couples therapy. They can guide you further on healthy coping strategies tailored to your specific needs as a couple.

6. Create New Rituals: In addition to participating in bereavement support groups, consider creating new rituals or routines as a couple. This could involve dedicating specific moments each day to reflect on your emotions or scheduling regular date nights or outings to create positive memories together amidst the grief.

7. Utilize Online Communities: The digital world offers a wealth of resources, including online forums and communities where you can connect with others who have experienced similar losses within their marriage. Sharing your experiences and listening to the experiences of others may provide comfort and validation.

Remember, healing takes time, and grief is not linear. Some days will be harder than others, but by implementing these strategies and seeking support from one another, you can navigate this grieving process together while strengthening your bond as a couple.

I've been feeling overwhelmed with the expectation of hosting lunch for our friends every week. The pressure to provide a perfect meal and make everyone feel included is taking a toll on me. I've even started to dread the thought of hosting, which is unfortunate because I genuinely enjoy it. It's not just the cooking and preparation that's causing stress, but also the fear of letting people down or making someone feel excluded if we can't host them every week.

I can see how much joy and satisfaction you derive from hosting lunches for your friends, but it's crucial to recognize that the current pace is unsustainable and causing you significant stress. I'd like to propose a few strategies to help you manage these feelings and reduce the pressure you're experiencing.

First, let's explore the idea of setting realistic expectations. It's essential to remember that you can't please everyone all the time, and it's okay to prioritize your own well-being over the expectations of others. One potential solution could be to host lunches less frequently, perhaps every other week or so. This way, you can still enjoy the experience of hosting while also reducing the stress and anxiety it causes you.

Another option could be to delegate some of the responsibilities. For instance, you could ask your friends to bring a dish to share, which would alleviate the pressure of having to prepare and provide food for everyone yourself. This not only lightens your load but also fosters a sense of community and collaboration.

Lastly, it's essential to address the underlying feelings of guilt and fear of letting people down. It's natural to want to make everyone feel included and valued, but it's important to remember that you can't control others' reactions or feelings. Instead, focus on your intentions and the effort you put into hosting lunches, rather than the outcome.

In summary, my approach would be to help you set realistic expectations, delegate responsibilities, and address the underlying feelings of guilt and fear. By implementing these strategies, you'll be able to reduce the stress and anxiety associated with hosting lunches while still maintaining the joy and satisfaction it brings you.

Remember, it's essential to prioritize your own well-being and set boundaries when necessary. The goal is to find a balance that allows you to enjoy the experience of hosting lunches while also managing the associated stress and anxiety.

I’ve been in a long distance relationship with my girlfriend for just over a year. This past week she admitted to me that she has feelings for another guy. She says it’s “just a crush” but I don't know how to cope with it.    How should I deal with this?

Thanks for writing in. Several things come to mind:I don't know how you are communicating, but there is a great deal of difference between communicating through videoconferencing compared to text message when discussing subjects like this. Being able to hear and/or see each other will help you to be able to gauge a lot of the emotions connected to what is going on.Are you in a place where you can ask your girlfriend questions about this crush and actually listen to her answers? If you can listen non-defensively and ask questions about what is actually going on (kind of like an investigative reporter might), you are likely to hear about her experience, thoughts, feelings, etc., so you can actually see what the crush is like for her and how you want to react to that.Then you could see if she is willing to listen to your questions and answer them for you.Another tip: Find out when is a good time to have this conversation. If you are talking to your girlfriend after she just worked a 10 hour shift and she is frustrated about that, it is likely that the emotion will transfer to the conversation that you are having even though it doesn't have anything to do with that.Find a way to keep yourself grounded and centered during the conversation. Notice your feet on the floor or your hips in the chair. Mindfully play with an object or something like a paperclip or a pen. Doing this mindfully (by being aware of your senses) will help you to not feel so overwhelmed during the conversation.After you have more details, communicate about what it is that you want or wish for. It is often easier to hear and discuss as opposed to talking about something that you need.Remember that while anger is a very real emotion, there is always something else under it. Be aware of what else could be there: hurt, disappointment, betrayal, fear, etc.

I would use Swagger editor to define those contracts, and I would write the APIs to match interactions implied in mock-ups. I would vet the design with the team, I would walk through scenarios to see if the API would fit the use case and would not introduce performance bottlenecks, and I would simulate and automate as much as I could along the journey.

I was very careful to get it right the first time. It was never perfect the first time, of course. So, I also had to consider how the API could evolve while minimizing costs/impact to the rest of the system. The API, once deployed, would become something I would guard, like an honest politician guards the #usconstitution. The team had to be careful with any change that impacted the API.

API Mesh... More like API mess!
APIs rely on APIs which rely on more APIs and libraries. Once a system gets large enough, that complexity becomes a bottleneck. Small changes can have a huge ripple effect. Some approaches (like federated #GraphQL) help manage this complexity nicely. But it still involves an API under which there can exist a lot of fragility. #Agile or not, developing a complicated web of APIs is complex, requires specialized skills, and is full of unforeseen challenges.

The Kitchen Conversation, ChatGPT-style
The Jetsons' kitchen involves a number of systems, each composed of various parts, sensors, hardware, inputs and outputs. Considering the complexity of interactions between independent systems in a kitchen, the fact that the Jetsons' kitchen components would come from various vendors or manufacturers, traditional API design would not be able to fulfill the vision. Not practical, at all.

Now, let's think about APIs and the Jetsons' kitchen, #chatgpt -style.

Let's keep it simple: pizza. You (or your robot) make a pizza from scratch.

The oven asks the refrigerator: "I see we have a pizza. Can you tell me if this is low-moisture mozzarella?"

Refrigerator: "That's not even mozzarella. This pizza must have Muenster cheese as that is all I had in me. And the human removed some of the contents 30 minutes ago, so the probability of Muenster cheese on that pizza is quite high."

A sensor from the kitchen who has eyes across the room chimes in at this point. Sensor: "Beware that the crust of this pizza is made of cauliflower. I agree with the video sensor's assessment regarding the type of cheese. No new cheese entered the kitchen recently."

Oven: "Anything else I should know?"

Sensor: "The temperature of the dough is 47F. This is cooler than the expert chef consensus of using room-temperature dough."

Oven: "Great. I know what to do. Since the dough is cool, I will start cooking with a temperature a little lower than the recipe specifies. Then I will increase the temp of bottom element so as to provide a nice crisp crust. I will keep a close eye on moisture and may use convection to mitigate any undesirable levels of moisture."

Where is the API that contractually binds the independent systems? APIs are not gone. For instance, the brain of the Oven will have myriad APIs (e.g. for interacting with temperature controllers and sensors, etc.). The key here is that the interface between systems is no longer a fixed, rigid API. No method signatures, no paths, no payload specifications. Instead, a conversation relating to senses and capabilities.

What "brain"?
Kence Anderson's book Designing Autonomous AI describes nicely how a complex system can be decomposed into a number of independent "brains." Each brain, in his book, can be independently developed and refined, with human guidance married with #datascience, #machinelearning and #dataengineering.

What's Cookin'?
I am excited for what the future holds. How architects rethink complex system design with regards to APIs is, in my opinion, something that is inevitable. And, as an amateur pizza maker, my taste buds are watering for the day I get some GPT help to make an even better #detroitpizza.

Excessive stress has taken a toll on my overall well-being. It manifests in various forms, such as headaches, digestive issues, and difficulty sleeping. I want to reduce the impact of stress on my physical health by finding healthy coping mechanisms and learning how to manage stressful situations more effectively.

Stress can indeed have a significant impact on both our physical and mental well-being. It's great that you're looking for ways to reduce the impact of stress on your overall health. Here are some suggestions and guidance:

1. Start by practicing relaxation techniques: Incorporate activities like deep breathing exercises, meditation, or progressive muscle relaxation into your daily routine. These techniques can help calm your mind and body during stressful situations.

2. Engage in regular physical activity: Exercise has been shown to be an effective stress reducer. Find activities that you enjoy, such as walking, dancing, yoga, or any other form of exercise that gets your body moving. Regular exercise releases endorphins, which are natural mood boosters that can alleviate stress.

3. Prioritize self-care: Make sure you are taking care of yourself physically, mentally, and emotionally. This includes getting enough sleep, eating nutritious meals, and setting aside time for activities you enjoy. Treat yourself with kindness and compassion.

4. Create structure and establish boundaries: Organize your day and set realistic goals for yourself. Establishing boundaries at work, home, and in relationships can help reduce stress by creating a sense of control and balance. Learn to say no when necessary and prioritize your needs.

5. Seek support from loved ones: Reach out to friends or family members who can provide a listening ear or offer helpful advice. Sharing your feelings and experiences with trusted individuals can provide a sense of connection and support.

6. Practice positive thinking: Challenge negative thoughts and replace them with more positive and realistic perspectives. Focus on gratitude and try to find something positive in each day. Surround yourself with uplifting and supportive people and engage in activities that bring you joy.

7. Consider implementing stress-management techniques: Explore different techniques that resonate with you, such as journaling, listening to calming music, engaging in hobbies, or even connecting with nature. The idea is to find healthy outlets that help you relax and unwind.

Remember, managing stress is an ongoing process. It may take time to find the strategies that work best for you. Be patient with yourself, and don't be afraid to seek additional support from mental health professionals if needed. You're taking a proactive step towards better well-being by recognizing the impact of stress and seeking healthier coping mechanisms. Keep up the positive attitude!

I've been struggling with feelings of guilt and sadness ever since I moved my father into an assisted living facility. I used to promise him that he wouldn't have to leave his home, and I would reassure him by describing the street sign outside his window. But now I realize that I was probably causing him more anxiety by not telling him the truth about where he was. I feel like I've failed him in some way, and I can't shake off these feelings of regret.

Your feelings of guilt and sadness are understandable given the circumstances. It's natural to feel a sense of responsibility and attachment to a parent, especially when they are facing the challenges of aging and cognitive decline. In your case, you believed that by describing the familiar street sign, you were providing comfort and reassurance to your father. However, you now recognize that your actions may have inadvertently increased his anxiety by not telling him the truth about his location. This is a common challenge in caring for loved ones with dementia or other cognitive impairments. It's essential to find a balance between maintaining their sense of familiarity and reality, while also being truthful and transparent about their circumstances.

Your feelings of guilt and sadness are not only a response to your father's current situation but also a reflection of your past promises and the emotional bond you share. It's important to acknowledge these feelings and allow yourself to grieve the loss of your father's independence and the changes that have come with his move to the assisted living facility.

In future interactions, consider agreeing with your father about his current location or focusing on the present moment, rather than trying to reassure him with false information. This approach can help reduce his anxiety and promote a sense of calm and security. Additionally, consider engaging in activities that bring joy and comfort to both you and your father, such as reminiscing about past memories or sharing stories. These moments can help strengthen your bond and provide a sense of connection despite the physical distance.

It's also essential to take care of yourself during this time. Caring for a loved one with cognitive impairments can be emotionally and physically demanding, and it's crucial to maintain your own well-being to be able to provide the best care possible. Consider seeking support from friends, family, or support groups to help manage the emotional challenges of caregiving.

In summary, your feelings of guilt and sadness are valid and complex, and it's essential to find a balance between maintaining your father's sense of familiarity and reality, while also being truthful and transparent about his circumstances. By focusing on the present moment and engaging in activities that bring joy and comfort to both you and your father, you can help reduce his anxiety and promote a sense of calm and security, while also taking care of yourself during this challenging time.

Learning to forgive ourselves and others is so important. I've always had a tendency to worry, but these days my anxiety seems to be at an all-time high. Even everyday situations trigger intense feelings of fear and nervousness. For example, before leaving the house, I obsessively check if I turned off appliances or locked the doors multiple times to ensure everything is safe. These rituals consume a significant amount of time and energy, making me late for appointments and increasing my stress further. I recognize that these behaviors are irrational, yet they seem impossible to resist. I desire guidance on how to overcome these anxiety-driven compulsions and regain control over my life.

It sounds like you're experiencing a lot of anxiety and it's having a significant impact on your daily life. It can be really challenging to feel overwhelmed by worries and compulsive behaviors. I want to reassure you that you're not alone in this, and there are strategies you can try to help manage your anxiety.

One technique you might find helpful is called "thought stopping." When you catch yourself obsessively checking appliances or doors, try mentally telling yourself "stop" or "enough" to interrupt the compulsion. You can also redirect your attention to something else, like taking deep breaths or focusing on an object in your surroundings.

Another approach is to gradually expose yourself to situations that trigger your anxiety, starting with less intense situations and working your way up. This process, known as exposure therapy, can help reduce your fear over time. For example, you could start by intentionally leaving one appliance on while you're out and gradually increase the number over weeks or months.

Practicing relaxation techniques, such as deep breathing exercises or progressive muscle relaxation, can also help calm your mind and body when anxiety strikes. Finding activities that bring you joy and help distract from anxious thoughts, such as engaging in hobbies or spending time with loved ones, can also be beneficial.

Additionally, creating a structured routine may provide a sense of control and security for you. Breaking tasks into smaller, manageable steps and setting realistic goals can help prevent feeling overwhelmed. Prioritizing self-care activities like getting plenty of sleep, eating well, and exercising regularly can also assist in managing anxiety symptoms.

Although these strategies might be helpful, it's important to remember that they may not eliminate your anxiety completely, and seeking support from a mental health professional can offer additional guidance tailored to your specific needs. Therapy sessions can provide a safe space to explore the underlying causes of your anxiety and develop personalized coping mechanisms.

Remember, overcoming anxiety takes time and patience, so don't be too hard on yourself. With practice and support, you can regain control over your life and find ways to manage your anxiety-driven compulsions more effectively.

I've been taking care of my mother in the hospital for some time now, and I've noticed that she hasn't shown any signs of distress, such as labored breathing, hyperventilation, negative vocalization, or facial expressions that suggest sadness or tension. She has been smiling and appears relaxed. I'm worried that she might be hiding her pain or discomfort, and I don't know how to approach the situation without causing her any more distress.

Your concern for your mother's wellbeing is commendable. It's natural to feel worried when we suspect that someone we care about might be experiencing pain or discomfort that they're not expressing openly. In situations like these, it's essential to approach the conversation with sensitivity, empathy, and a non-judgmental attitude. Begin by expressing your concern for her wellbeing and let her know that you've noticed some changes in her behavior that have left you feeling uneasy. Be specific about the observations you've made and avoid making assumptions or jumping to conclusions. Instead, invite her to share her feelings and experiences, and create a safe and supportive environment where she feels comfortable expressing herself.

It's also important to remember that people often hide their pain or discomfort due to various reasons, such as fear, embarrassment, or a belief that they're burdening others. In such cases, it might be helpful to validate her feelings and let her know that it's okay to express her emotions, and that you're there to support her through this difficult time. Encourage her to share her thoughts and feelings, and offer your listening ear and unwavering support.

Additionally, it might be helpful to explore the possibility that her current situation might be triggering past traumas or unresolved emotional issues. If this is the case, it might be beneficial to consider engaging in therapeutic interventions, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy, mindfulness practices, or psychotherapy, to help her process and heal from these experiences.

Throughout this process, it's crucial to maintain ethical and professional standards, ensuring that her privacy and confidentiality are respected, and that her autonomy and self-determination are upheld. Remember, the ultimate goal is to create a safe and supportive environment where she feels heard, understood, and empowered to express her emotions and work through her challenges.

How do you know you have the right therapist for you?
 How would I know how to "train" my therapist to be able to give me what I need from treatment?

Such a good question!  Sometimes, clients will feel like they are not connecting with their therapist and will put it on themselves.  In truth, the bond between therapist and client is the #1 predictor of positive outcomes in therapy.  Ask yourself these questions: does it feel like this person can come to care about me?  Do they remember from week to week what we touched on?  Do I feel compassion from this person? Do they allow me my difficult and painful feelings too, or do they try to rescue me?  On your other question - I suggest you ask your therapist what goals he/she has for your treatment.  See if they respond with interest and participation, or if they become clinical and distant.  Ideally, you and your therapist jointly develop your goals, and check on your progress on a frequent basis.  I don't know if you can actually 'train' your therapist - we can be a hard bunch to train! :-)  - but you can definitely tell your therapist what works for you, and what didn't work, at the end of each session.  How they react will also tell you a lot about whether this is the right person for you.

"My close friendships have become strained lately due to misunderstandings and conflicts. I want to repair these relationships because they mean a lot to me. Is there any advice or strategies you can provide to enhance my communication skills and rebuild trust with my friends?"

Building and maintaining healthy relationships can indeed require effort and effective communication skills. Here are some guidance and strategies that may help enhance your communication skills and rebuild trust with your friends:

1. Reflect on the misunderstandings and conflicts: Take some time to reflect on what might have caused these issues in your friendships. Consider your own role in the misunderstandings and conflicts, as it's important to take responsibility for any part you played. This introspection can help you gain insight into your communication patterns and identify areas for improvement.

2. Open and honest conversations: Initiate open and honest conversations with your friends about the strained relationships. Express your desire to repair these bonds and clarify any misunderstandings that may exist. Create a safe space where both parties feel comfortable expressing their thoughts and feelings without judgment. Active listening is key during these conversations – truly hear what they have to say and try to understand their perspective.

3. Apologize and make amends if necessary: If you realize that you've made mistakes or contributed to the conflicts, offer sincere apologies to your friends. Acknowledge your behavior and express genuine remorse. Making amends may involve taking concrete actions to rectify the situation or address any harm caused. Your friends will likely appreciate your efforts to reconcile.

4. Improve your communication skills: Effective communication involves more than just speaking; it also includes active listening and empathy. Practice active listening by giving your full attention when others speak, asking clarifying questions, and summarizing what you've heard to ensure understanding. Show empathy by placing yourself in their shoes and acknowledging their emotions.

5. Manage conflict constructively: Conflicts may still arise even in close friendships. It's essential to learn how to manage them constructively. Instead of avoiding or escalating conflicts, approach them head-on with a problem-solving mindset. Focus on finding common ground, compromising when necessary, and seeking resolutions that respect everyone's needs and boundaries.

6. Foster trust and understanding: Rebuilding trust takes time and consistency. Be reliable and follow through on your commitments to demonstrate dependability. Show empathy and understanding towards your friends' experiences, validating their emotions without judgment. Trust can grow when you consistently act with integrity and maintain open lines of communication.

7. Prioritize self-reflection and personal growth: As you work on enhancing your communication skills, don't forget the importance of self-reflection and personal growth. Take time to examine your own values, beliefs, and triggers that may impact your relationships. Consider seeking personal development resources such as books, workshops, or online courses, which can provide valuable insights into effective communication and maintaining healthy friendships.

Remember, rebuilding strained relationships takes patience and effort from both sides. While these strategies can aid in enhancing your communication skills, it's essential to allow space for your friends to participate actively in the relationship repair process.

I've recently started counseling, but I'm feeling unsure about the process and what to expect. Sometimes I question if it's really helping me or if I'm just wasting my time. I'd like to understand more about the fundamentals of counseling and how it can benefit me in the long run. What are some strategies or techniques that therapists commonly use? How can I make the most out of my counseling sessions?

I'm glad to hear that you've started counseling! It's completely normal to feel unsure about the process and have questions about its effectiveness. Counseling can be a valuable tool for personal growth and emotional well-being.

To help you understand the fundamentals of counseling, it's important to know that therapists are trained professionals who provide a safe and non-judgmental space for you to explore your thoughts, feelings, and experiences. They aim to support you in gaining insight into yourself, developing coping skills, and making positive changes in your life.

Therapists use various strategies and techniques tailored to your specific needs and goals. Some common approaches include cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), which focuses on identifying and changing negative thought patterns; psychodynamic therapy, which explores unconscious influences on behavior; and person-centered therapy, which emphasizes empathy and understanding.

In addition to these approaches, therapists may also utilize mindfulness techniques, relaxation exercises, journaling, or art therapy, depending on what resonates with you. These methods can help you gain self-awareness, manage stress, improve communication skills, and develop healthier coping mechanisms.

To make the most out of your counseling sessions, here are some suggestions:

1. Be open and honest: Share your thoughts, feelings, and concerns openly with your therapist. Honesty is crucial for building trust and creating a productive therapeutic relationship.

2. Set goals: Reflect on what you hope to achieve through counseling and discuss these goals with your therapist. This will help guide your sessions and give you a sense of direction.

3. Take an active role: Therapy is a collaborative process, so actively participate by asking questions, seeking clarification, and sharing any insights or observations you have between sessions.

4. Practice self-care: Engage in activities that promote your overall well-being outside of therapy. This could include exercise, hobbies, spending time with loved ones, or practicing relaxation techniques.

5. Be patient and give it time: Personal growth takes time, so don't expect immediate results. Trust the process and be open to exploring different strategies with your therapist.

Remember, counseling is a journey unique to each individual, and what works for one person may not work for another. It's important to find a therapist who you feel comfortable with and who aligns with your needs and values. Keep an open mind, stay committed to the process, and trust that positive changes can happen over time.

Hi Greenville, I respect that you're owning your own overreactions, and that you want to give your boyfriend the respect he deserves. The truth is that some people cheat, and some don't, and our partners deserve the benefit of the doubt unless they show signs they can't be trusted.The answer here is in two different areas. Basically, if you want to feel differently (more trusting, in your case), you look at your thoughts, and your behaviours.Your thoughts are stuck... like tires in deep ruts in the road. These thoughts are only habits, they don't reflect the truth. Fear is probably whispering in your ear things like "everyone cheats", or " you're not enough for him". Once you figure out what fear is trying to tell you, picture those words in red next time they come up. Ask yourself what the evidence is that supports that thought (there won't be much...perhaps none), and what is the evidence that doesn't support it (I know lots of good men, I know I deserve love and loyalty, there is no sign of infidelity...). You're learning to refute the thoughts that are connected to the fear. That's the first half. Practise these thoughts.The rest of the work is in your behaviours. Act as though you trust him. Force yourself to not check or interrogate, and the less you check, the less obsessive and untrusting you will feel. Acting "as if" something if true strangely helps us believe it.It's possible to change the way we think, and this is turn changes the way we feel.
